ideas.hypothesis: Countries electing legislatures by proportional representation run more procyclical fiscal policy, because coalition common-pool problems make it harder to save revenue windfalls in booms.
ideas.test: Panel of ~80 countries 1980-2015: estimate country-specific cyclicality coefficients (government spending growth on output gap) and regress them on electoral-system dummies (Database of Political Institutions), controlling for institutional quality and resource dependence.
ideas.disconfirming: Proportional-representation countries show equal or less procyclical spending than majoritarian countries after controls.

ideas.hypothesis: Government spending multipliers are larger in countries with higher institutional quality, because less spending leaks into rents and procurement waste.
ideas.test: Panel local projections of output on identified spending shocks for ~50 countries, interacting the shock with World Governance Indicators (government effectiveness, control of corruption); compare cumulative two-year multipliers across terciles.
ideas.disconfirming: Multipliers do not increase, or decrease, with institutional quality.

ideas.hypothesis: Expenditure-based fiscal consolidations in the EU new member states raised income inequality through wage compression, whereas revenue-based consolidations did not.
ideas.test: Use the identified consolidation episodes for the new member states (1995-2015) and estimate panel local projections of the Gini coefficient (EU-SILC/SWIID) and labor share, split by expenditure- vs revenue-based composition.
ideas.disconfirming: Gini and labor share do not change after expenditure-based consolidations, or change equally after revenue-based ones.

ideas.hypothesis: New EU member states with smaller automatic stabilizers (lower semi-elasticity of the budget balance to output) experienced larger output volatility and deeper 2009 recessions.
ideas.test: Compute budget semi-elasticities for the 11 new member states from OECD/EC methodology; correlate with output-gap volatility 2000-2015 and the 2009 output decline, controlling for trade openness.
ideas.disconfirming: Countries with larger stabilizers show equal or greater output volatility and recession depth.

ideas.hypothesis: Fiscal multipliers are larger during deflationary periods because spending raises inflation expectations and lowers real interest rates when nominal rates are constrained.
ideas.test: State-dependent local projections on a panel of OECD countries plus China and Japan, 1980-2018, interacting spending shocks with a deflation-regime indicator (negative core CPI inflation).
ideas.disconfirming: Multipliers in deflationary regimes are not higher than in positive-inflation regimes.

ideas.hypothesis: Governments that financed wars mainly with bonds rather than money issuance subsequently ran primary surpluses consistent with the intertemporal budget constraint, while money-financed wars were followed by breakdowns in debt-surplus cointegration.
ideas.test: Historical annual fiscal data for Australia, the US, UK and others across 20th-century wars; apply structural-break cointegration tests of revenue and expenditure separately for bond-financed and money-financed war episodes.
ideas.disconfirming: Post-war fiscal behaviour satisfies the budget constraint equally regardless of the financing mix.

ideas.hypothesis: In small post-communist economies, transfer-based fiscal expansions raise household consumption, unlike government purchases, because transfers target liquidity-constrained households.
ideas.test: SVAR or local projections on quarterly Romanian and regional new-member-state data 2000-2019, separating shocks to social transfers from shocks to government consumption, with private consumption as outcome.
ideas.disconfirming: Household consumption responds no more to transfer shocks than to purchase shocks.

ideas.hypothesis: Delegating part of fiscal stabilization to an independent body (fiscal council or delegated tax-rate adjustment) reduces the procyclicality of discretionary fiscal policy.
ideas.test: Difference-in-differences on ~40 countries 1990-2018 using IMF fiscal council dataset adoption dates; outcome is the rolling cyclicality coefficient of the cyclically adjusted primary balance.
ideas.disconfirming: Cyclicality does not fall after fiscal council adoption relative to non-adopters.

ideas.hypothesis: Higher reliance on value added tax in revenue makes revenue swings more procyclical in transition economies, which under deficit targets translates into procyclical spending cuts in downturns.
ideas.test: Estimate revenue-to-output elasticities by tax type for Romania, Ukraine and other Central/Eastern European countries 2000-2018; relate the VAT revenue share to spending cyclicality in a cross-country panel.
ideas.disconfirming: VAT-reliant countries show no larger revenue elasticity or no more procyclical spending.

ideas.hypothesis: EU countries with higher pre-2010 energy tax shares were able to carry out revenue-based fiscal consolidations with smaller output losses, because energy tax increases are less distortionary than labor tax increases.
ideas.test: Panel of EU-28 consolidation episodes 2009-2015 (narrative data); regress two-year output response on the share of consolidation achieved through energy taxes, controlling for size and timing.
ideas.disconfirming: Energy-tax-heavy consolidations show output losses at least as large as other revenue-based consolidations.

ideas.hypothesis: Fiscal multipliers in small open economies fall sharply once public debt exceeds roughly 60% of GDP, because higher sovereign risk premia offset the spending impulse.
ideas.test: Threshold panel VAR for ~30 small open economies, including Romania, 1995-2018, with debt-to-GDP as threshold variable and sovereign spreads included.
ideas.disconfirming: Multipliers do not differ between high- and low-debt regimes.

ideas.hypothesis: Fiscal policy in resource-rich Sub-Saharan African countries violated the intertemporal budget constraint before debt relief initiatives but satisfied it afterwards, with structural breaks aligned to HIPC completion points.
ideas.test: Country-by-country cointegration tests of revenue and expenditure with endogenous structural breaks (Gregory-Hansen) for ~25 SSA countries 1970-2015.
ideas.disconfirming: No structural breaks near debt relief dates, or no change in sustainability status.

ideas.hypothesis: Greater fiscal transparency reduces procyclical spending in good times by limiting voters' asymmetric information about revenue windfalls.
ideas.test: Panel of developing countries 2006-2018 using the Open Budget Index; regress spending cyclicality in booms on transparency scores, with country and year fixed effects.
ideas.disconfirming: Transparency scores have no association with boom-period spending cyclicality.

ideas.hypothesis: Fiscal consolidations disproportionately cut R&D subsidies, and these cuts reduce business R&D and patenting for several years, offsetting part of the consolidation's long-run fiscal gain.
ideas.test: OECD panel 1990-2016: identify consolidation episodes; estimate responses of government budget appropriations for R&D, business R&D expenditure and patents via local projections.
ideas.disconfirming: R&D subsidies are cut no more than other spending, or business R&D does not decline after consolidations.

ideas.hypothesis: R&D tax incentives crowd in private R&D, whereas direct government investment crowds out private investment, so the composition of fiscal support determines net private investment response.
ideas.test: Chinese provincial panel 2000-2015: regress private fixed investment and private R&D on provincial tax-incentive intensity and public investment, using IS-LM-based crowding coefficients estimated with instrumental variables.
ideas.disconfirming: Tax incentives also reduce private investment, or public investment raises it.

ideas.hypothesis: Spending multipliers are smaller when uncertainty about future fiscal consolidation timing and composition is high, because households and firms defer spending.
ideas.test: State-dependent local projections for EU countries 2000-2018 using an economic policy uncertainty index (or fiscal-news dispersion) as the state variable.
ideas.disconfirming: Multipliers do not vary with fiscal policy uncertainty.

ideas.hypothesis: Under a supranational central bank, the strategic Nash interaction between monetary and national fiscal authorities produces larger sovereign spread spikes than in countries with a national central bank, for given debt levels.
ideas.test: Compare euro-area periphery with non-euro EU and other advanced economies 2008-2013: panel regression of sovereign spreads on debt and deficits, interacting with a monetary-union dummy.
ideas.disconfirming: Spread sensitivity to debt is no larger for monetary-union members.

ideas.hypothesis: Higher transport taxes reduce per-capita car travel more in compact urban areas, where alternatives exist, than in dispersed areas.
ideas.test: Panel of European metropolitan areas: vehicle-kilometres per capita regressed on national transport tax rates interacted with urban density measures, 2000-2016.
ideas.disconfirming: Transport tax effects on car travel are equal across urban forms or zero.

ideas.hypothesis: Chinese provinces that expanded rural education spending more after the fiscal policy transition narrowed urban-rural income gaps more over the following decade.
ideas.test: Provincial panel 2000-2015: regress urban-rural income ratio on lagged rural education expenditure per pupil, with province and year fixed effects and instrumenting with central transfer formulas.
ideas.disconfirming: Rural education spending has no effect on the urban-rural income gap.

ideas.hypothesis: In Romania and comparable new member states, the structural deficit widens systematically in election years, explaining a large part of observed fiscal procyclicality.
ideas.test: Panel of new member states 2000-2018: regress the change in structural deficit on election-year dummies, controlling for output gap and EU program status.
ideas.disconfirming: No significant widening of the structural deficit in election years.

ideas.hypothesis: Hierarchical clustering of countries on structural features (resource dependence, institutional quality, borrowing access) yields groups whose fiscal cyclicality differs more sharply than regional groupings do.
ideas.test: Cluster ~100 countries on structural indicators; compare between-cluster variance in estimated spending cyclicality to that across standard geographic regions.
ideas.disconfirming: Clusters explain no more cyclicality variance than geographic regions.

ideas.hypothesis: Expenditure-based fiscal consolidations in current-account-deficit countries reduce external imbalances mainly through export growth rather than import compression.
ideas.test: Panel local projections for ~40 countries of exports and imports (% GDP) after narrative consolidation shocks, split by initial current account balance.
ideas.disconfirming: The external adjustment comes from import compression, or there is none.

ideas.hypothesis: Adopting medium-term budget forecasting and indicative planning reduces deviations between planned and executed budgets.
ideas.test: Cross-country PEFA scores for budget credibility (aggregate expenditure outturn) before and after medium-term framework adoption, in a difference-in-differences design.
ideas.disconfirming: Budget execution deviations do not shrink after medium-term framework adoption.

ideas.hypothesis: Procyclical fiscal policy during credit booms amplifies financial instability, so countries with more procyclical pre-2008 fiscal stances suffered larger non-performing loan increases after 2008.
ideas.test: Cross-section of ~40 emerging and advanced economies: regress the 2008-2012 rise in NPL ratios on the 2004-2008 fiscal cyclicality coefficient, controlling for credit growth.
ideas.disconfirming: Pre-crisis fiscal procyclicality is unrelated to NPL increases.

ideas.hypothesis: Reductions in fiscal pressure on firms (lower effective tax burden) increase export growth in small open transition economies by improving cost competitiveness.
ideas.test: Firm-level or sector-level panel for Romania and peers 2002-2016 relating changes in effective tax rates to export growth, with sector fixed effects.
ideas.disconfirming: Export growth does not respond to changes in fiscal pressure.

ideas.hypothesis: Fiscal policy effectiveness in Serbia and similar economies is greater during periods of exchange rate stability than during periods of high volatility.
ideas.test: Regime-switching VAR on quarterly Serbian data 2003-2018, with the regime defined by exchange-rate volatility; compare output responses to fiscal shocks.
ideas.disconfirming: Fiscal effectiveness is similar or higher in high-volatility regimes.

ideas.hypothesis: Excessive deficit procedures under the Stability and Growth Pact reduced headline deficits mainly through one-off measures, leaving structural deficits largely unchanged.
ideas.test: EU panel 2000-2018: compare changes in headline vs structural deficits during excessive deficit procedure years vs other years.
ideas.disconfirming: Structural deficits fall as much as headline deficits during excessive deficit procedures.

ideas.hypothesis: Household consumption becomes less responsive to fiscal shocks as public debt rises, consistent with stronger Ricardian behavior at high debt levels.
ideas.test: Panel VAR with interaction between fiscal shocks and debt-to-GDP for EU countries 1995-2018; outcome is private consumption and household saving.
ideas.disconfirming: Consumption responses do not decline with higher public debt.

ideas.hypothesis: Municipalities adopting smart growth policies require less per-capita public investment in roads and utilities.
ideas.test: US municipal panel 1990-2015: compare per-capita capital outlays before and after smart growth ordinance adoption against matched non-adopters.
ideas.disconfirming: Per-capita public investment does not fall, or rises, after smart growth adoption.

ideas.hypothesis: The value of Confederate paper money moved with expectations of fiscal backing, so military news that changed the expected likelihood of future tax revenue predicted note depreciation.
ideas.test: Time series of Confederate note prices in gold (1861-1865) regressed on coded battle outcomes and fiscal legislation events.
ideas.disconfirming: Note values do not respond to news that alters expected fiscal backing.
